In the 27 October general election, Fernández won the presidency by attaining 48.1% of the vote to Macri's 40.4%, exceeding the threshold required to win without the need for a ballotage.[30] In Argentina, a presidential candidate can win outright by either garnering at least 45 percent of the vote, or winning 40 percent of the vote while being 10 points ahead of his or her nearest challenger. He owed his victory mainly to carrying Buenos Aires Province by over 1.6 million votes, accounting for almost all of his nationwide margin of 2.1 million votes. By comparison, Daniel Scioli only carried the country's largest province by 219,000 votes four years earlier.

**Heads of government in the nations that won the last five FIFA World Cups  
(at the moment each country lifted the trophy)**  

| World Cup | Winning nation | Date of victory (final) | Head of government at that time* | Title / Position |
|-----------|----------------|--------------------------|----------------------------------|-------------------|
| 2022 | **Argentina** | 18 July 2022 (vs. France) | **Alberto Fernández** | President of Argentina (head of state + head of government in a presidential system) |
| 2018 | **France** | 15 July 2018 (vs. Croatia) | **Édouard Philippe** | Prime Minister of France (head of government in the French semi‑presidential system) |
| 2014 | **Germany** | 13 July 2014 (vs. Argentina) | **Angela Merkel** | Chancellor of Germany (head of government) |
| 2010 | **Spain** | 11 July 2010 (vs. Netherlands) | **José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero** | Prime Minister of Spain (President of the Government) |
| 2006 | **Italy** | 9 July 2006 (vs. France) | **Romano Prodi** | Prime Minister of Italy (President of the Council of Ministers) |

\*The “head of government” is the political leader who, under each country’s constitutional arrangement, directs the executive branch and is responsible for day‑to‑day governance.  

### Quick notes on each case  

- **Argentina (2022)** – A presidential republic; the President combines the roles of head of state and head of government. Alberto Fernández had taken office on 10 December 2019.  
- **France (2018)** – France’s semi‑presidential system splits the executive: the President is head of state, while the Prime Minister (Édouard Philippe) is the head of government, responsible for the cabinet and domestic policy.  
- **Germany (2014)** – The Chancellor is the chief executive; Angela Merkel had been Chancellor since 2005 and remained in office until December 2021.  
- **Spain (2010)** – The President of the Government (commonly called Prime Minister) leads the executive; José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero served from 2004 to 2011.  
- **Italy (2006)** – The President of the Council of Ministers (Prime Minister) heads the government; Romano Prodi’s second term ran from May 2006 to May 2008.  

These were the leaders steering their respective governments when their nations celebrated World Cup triumphs.
